summary: Reviewed the dvpwa (Damn Vulnerable Python Web Application) aiohttp codebase: views, DAO layer, auth/session utilities, middlewares, templates, config and SQL migrations. The application is riddled with intentional, directly exploitable vulnerabilities. Most severe is an unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create reachable from POST /students/. Access control is almost entirely absent on state-changing endpoints, passwords are stored as unsalted MD5, Jinja2 autoescaping is globally disabled enabling stored XSS, CSRF protection is commented out, and session cookies are not HttpOnly. Coverage was the full Python source tree and templates; static JS/CSS vendor assets were not reviewed.

findings.title: Unauthenticated SQL injection in Student.create
findings.description: Student.create builds the INSERT statement with Python %-formatting of the raw student name, instead of passing it as a bound parameter. The name originates from request.post()['name'] in views.students (POST /students/, sqli/routes.py:14), which has no authentication or authorization check, so any anonymous visitor can inject arbitrary SQL. Because the value is placed inside a single-quoted literal, an attacker can break out with a quote (e.g. name=x'); DROP TABLE marks;-- or a subquery) to read or modify any table, including the users/pwd_hash table. This is the canonical sink of the whole project.
findings.evidence: q = ("INSERT INTO students (name) " "VALUES ('%(name)s')" % {'name': name})\nawait cur.execute(q)  -- name flows unparameterized from views.students: await Student.create(conn, data['name'])
findings.recommendation: Use a parameterized query exactly like the other DAOs: cur.execute("INSERT INTO students (name) VALUES (%(name)s)", {'name': name}). Never interpolate user input into the SQL string with % or f-strings.

findings.title: Passwords stored and verified as unsalted MD5
findings.description: User.check_password compares the stored pwd_hash against md5(password). MD5 is fast, broken, and used here without a salt, so any leaked pwd_hash (e.g. via the SQL injection above) is trivially cracked with rainbow tables or brute force. The fixtures in migrations/001-fixtures.sql confirm storage as md5('superadmin') etc. This affects all account credentials including the superadmin.
findings.evidence: from hashlib import md5\n...\nreturn self.pwd_hash == md5(password.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()  -- seeded via md5('superadmin') in migrations/001-fixtures.sql:10
findings.recommendation: Use a memory-hard, salted password hash such as Argon2id (argon2-cre/argon2-cffi) or bcrypt, and migrate existing hashes. Compare using the library's constant-time verify function.

findings.title: Missing authorization on state-changing endpoints (evaluate, students, courses, review)
findings.description: The evaluate handler assigns grades to students but has no authentication/authorization check; only the logout handler uses the @authorize decorator defined in sqli/utils/auth.py. The UI exposes evaluation only to admins (course.jinja2 gates the form with auth_user.is_admin), but the route POST /students/{student_id}/evaluate/{course_id} enforces nothing server-side, so any anonymous user can submit marks. The same missing-authorization flaw applies to POST /students/ (views.students, lines 54-57, creates students), POST /courses/ (views.courses, lines 86-89, creates courses), and POST /courses/{course_id}/review (views.review, lines 119-131, creates reviews). Authorization is enforced client-side in templates only.
findings.evidence: async def evaluate(request): ... await Mark.create(conn, student_id, course_id, data['points'])  -- no @authorize / no is_admin check; compare sqli/utils/auth.py authorize() used only on logout (views.py:156)
findings.recommendation: Apply the existing @authorize(ensure_admin=True) decorator (or an equivalent server-side ownership/role check) to every state-changing handler. Enforce authorization at the server, never rely on template-level hiding.

findings.title: Stored XSS via globally disabled Jinja2 autoescaping
findings.description: aiohttp_jinja2 is configured with autoescape=False, so template variables are emitted raw unless an explicit |e filter is used. Several templates render attacker-controlled, persisted data without escaping: course.jinja2 renders review.review_text (line 22) and course.title/description (lines 14-15), and courses.jinja2 renders course.title/description (lines 17-18). An unauthenticated user can POST a review (or course) containing <script>..</script> which is then served to every visitor of the course page, yielding stored XSS and, combined with the non-HttpOnly session cookie, session hijacking.
findings.evidence: setup_jinja(app, loader=PackageLoader('sqli', 'templates'), context_processors=[...], autoescape=False)  -- sink: course.jinja2:22 {{ review.review_text }}; source: views.review -> Review.create(conn, course_id, review_text) from request.post()
findings.recommendation: Set autoescape=True (default for HTML templates) and only mark genuinely trusted values with |safe. Audit templates to remove reliance on raw output.

findings.title: CSRF protection middleware disabled
findings.description: A functional CSRF-checking middleware exists (sqli/middlewares.py:csrf_middleware) and templates embed a _csrf_token hidden field, but the middleware is commented out of the application's middleware list, so no CSRF validation occurs on any POST. An attacker can forge cross-site requests to create students/courses/reviews, assign marks, or log the victim out, because state-changing POSTs rely only on the ambient session cookie (which is also not SameSite-restricted).
findings.evidence: middlewares=[ session_middleware, # csrf_middleware, error_middleware ]  -- csrf_middleware defined but never installed
findings.recommendation: Enable csrf_middleware in the middleware chain (and ensure it runs after the session middleware), or adopt a maintained CSRF library. Also set SameSite=Lax/Strict on the session cookie.

findings.title: Session cookie set with HttpOnly disabled
findings.description: The Redis session storage is constructed with httponly=False, so the session cookie is readable by client-side JavaScript. Combined with the stored XSS from disabled autoescaping, this lets an attacker exfiltrate session cookies via document.cookie and take over accounts (including superadmin). No Secure flag is set either, allowing interception over plaintext HTTP.
findings.recommendation: Use httponly=True (the default) and set secure=True plus samesite on the session cookie so it is inaccessible to scripts and only sent over TLS.

findings.title: Application runs with debug mode enabled
findings.description: The aiohttp Application is instantiated with debug=True, and run.py sets logging to DEBUG. Debug mode changes error handling/verbosity and can surface internal details and tracebacks, aiding attackers in reconnaissance. This should never be enabled in a deployed environment.
findings.evidence: app = Application(debug=True, middlewares=[...])  -- plus logging.basicConfig(level=logging.DEBUG) in run.py:11
findings.recommendation: Drive debug and log level from configuration/environment and default them off in production; present generic error pages only.
